sentences.text: Pachyornis was an extinct genus of flightless ratites from New Zealand belonging to the moa family, sharing a sternum lacking a keel, a trait common to all ratites.
This bird possessed a distinctive palate structure that set it apart from other members of its group.
While three species are currently recognized, two distinct genetic lineages found in the North and South Islands suggest the genus might eventually be expanded to five species.
P. elephantopus is considered the species with the most extreme morphology within the genus, resembling eastern moa but distinguished by a pointed bill and a heavier build.
Unlike its relatives, Pachyornis had a pointed bill rather than a broad one.
The species P. elephantopus exhibits the most extreme physical form known within the entire genus.
The genus Pachyornis was first described by Richard Lydekker in 1891.
Scientists have recorded 24 fossil occurrences of this bird in the Paleobiology Database.
Pachyornis species went extinct after human colonization of New Zealand, though P. australis may have died out earlier.
Pachyornis geranoides is the type species of the genus Pachyornis.
The parent group of the genus Pachyornis is the family Emeidae.
Fossils of Pachyornis date from the Gelasian epoch to the Holocene, spanning 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
